description_full: Quad/Graphics, Inc. provides marketing solutions in North America, Mexico, Central America, the Caribbean, Europe, the Middle East, Africa, South America, and Asia. The company operates through United States Print and Related Services, and International segments. It offers printing services, such as retail inserts, long-run publications, catalogs, special interest publications, journals, direct mail, directories, in-store marketing and promotion, packaging, newspapers, custom print products, and other commercial and specialty printed products; paper procurement services; and manufactures ink. The company also provides marketing and other services, including data intelligence and analytics, technology solutions, media planning, placement and optimization, creative strategy, and content creation, as well as execution in non-print digital and broadcast channels; and provides medical services. It serves blue-chip companies that operate in various industries and serve businesses and consumers across various industry verticals, including retail, consumer packaged goods and direct-to-consumer, financial services, and health. Quad/Graphics, Inc. was founded in 1971 and is headquartered in Sussex, Wisconsin.

financial_summary: Quad Graphics, Inc is a small-cap industrials business with a $387M market cap on $2.4B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at -9% over the past three years and -6% annually across the full decade, and a shrinking top line is the hardest headwind any business can overcome.
Returns on capital run at 4% against a 10% cost of capital, which means the business is destroying value with every dollar it reinvests.

The business throws off $51M in free cash flow — roughly 2 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 3.55× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, leverage is comfortably conservative at 1.8× net debt/EBITDA, and thin 1.9× interest coverage leaves no room for a bad year.

Management returns a meaningful 5.8% of market cap to owners through dividends and buybacks, a strong signal of disciplined capital allocation, and insiders hold 22% of the shares, so management thinks like owners because it is one — the strongest alignment there is, and profit capture is only 0.4× the fair share, suggesting no structural edge inside its industry.
